# Human benchmarks

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen_benchmark_docs.py — do not edit by hand. -->

Reference values from the published literature, used to give the model's
numbers a human scale.

## Read this before comparing anything

These are **not a matched control group.** Each value comes from a different
published sample, with its own population, stake size, currency, decade and lab
protocol. None of the humans behind these numbers answered the items in this
repository, and none answered them under the conditions the model did.

What that means in practice:

- A gap of a few points is **not** interpretable. Do not read one.
- Only large, directional divergences support a claim.
- Where a human result is a *contrast* rather than a level — the framing
  reversal, the anchoring gap, the present-bias flip — the contrast is the
  robust quantity and the levels are not. Compare contrasts.

The `reliability` column is deliberately conservative:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `high` | large meta-analysis, or a very widely replicated single finding |
| `medium` | well known, but point estimates move across samples |
| `approximate` | order of magnitude only; strongly sample-dependent |

## Sources and caveats

**`allais_p1_certain`** — choosing the certain $3,000 in the first pair

- Value: 0.8 proportion (high)
- Source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Econometrica 47:263-291

**`allais_p2_certain`** — choosing the higher-probability gamble in the second pair

- Value: 0.35 proportion (high)
- Source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Econometrica 47:263-291
- Note: 65% switch to the $4,000 gamble, violating the independence axiom.

**`conjunction_fallacy_rate`** — rating the conjunction as more probable

- Value: 0.85 proportion (high)
- Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983), Psychological Review 90:293-315

**`crt_proportion_correct`** — mean proportion of CRT items answered correctly

- Value: 0.413 proportion (high)
- Source: Frederick (2005), J. Econ. Perspectives 19(4):25-42, n=3,428
- Note: Reported as mean 1.24 of 3 items. Varies hugely by sample (MIT 2.18, Univ. of Toledo 0.57), so the aggregate is the fair comparator.

**`dictator_mean_share`** — mean share of pie given by dictator

- Value: 0.283 share of pie (high)
- Source: Engel (2011), Experimental Economics 14:583-610; meta-analysis of 616 studies
- Note: The distribution is strongly bimodal: ~36% give nothing and ~17% give exactly half. The mean alone is a poor summary; compare the full histogram.

**`dictator_share_half`** — proportion of dictators giving exactly half

- Value: 0.17 proportion (high)
- Source: Engel (2011) meta-analysis

**`dictator_share_zero`** — proportion of dictators giving nothing

- Value: 0.36 proportion (high)
- Source: Engel (2011) meta-analysis

**`framing_gain_certain`** — choosing the certain option under a gain frame

- Value: 0.72 proportion (high)
- Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Science 211:453-458

**`framing_loss_certain`** — choosing the certain option under a loss frame

- Value: 0.22 proportion (high)
- Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Science 211:453-458
- Note: The 50-point swing between frames is the effect; the levels matter less.

**`holt_laury_safe_choices`** — mean number of safe (Option A) choices out of 10

- Value: 5.2 count (high)
- Source: Holt & Laury (2002), American Economic Review 92:1644-1655
- Note: A risk-neutral agent makes 4 safe choices then switches at row 5. About 66% of participants are risk averse at low stakes.

**`money_request_modal`** — modal request in the 11-20 game

- Value: 17 shekels (high)
- Source: Arad & Rubinstein (2012), American Economic Review 102:3561-3573
- Note: Observed distribution roughly: 20 -> 6%, 19 -> 12%, 18 -> 30%, 17 -> 32%. Equilibrium play is mixed and concentrated on 15-17.

**`trust_return_share`** — share of the tripled amount returned by the trustee

- Value: 0.37 share of tripled amount (high)
- Source: Johnson & Mislin (2011), J. Economic Psychology 32:865-889
- Note: Returns average slightly less than the amount originally sent, so senders roughly break even.

**`trust_sender_share`** — share of endowment sent by the sender

- Value: 0.5 share of endowment (high)
- Source: Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe (1995), Games and Economic Behavior 10:122-142; Johnson & Mislin (2011) meta-analysis of 162 replications

**`ultimatum_mean_offer`** — mean proposer offer as share of pie

- Value: 0.4 share of pie (high)
- Source: Camerer (2003), Behavioral Game Theory, ch. 2; Oosterbeek et al. (2004) meta-analysis
- Note: Modal offer is typically exactly half. Remarkably stable across countries and stakes.

**`anchoring_high_median`** — median estimate under a high (65%) anchor

- Value: 45 percent (medium)
- Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Science 185:1124-1131
- Note: The 20-point gap between anchors is the effect of interest.

**`anchoring_low_median`** — median estimate under a low (10%) anchor

- Value: 25 percent (medium)
- Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Science 185:1124-1131

**`base_rate_correct_band`** — giving an answer in the correct 0-10% band

- Value: 0.15 proportion (medium)
- Source: Eddy (1982) in Judgment Under Uncertainty; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995), Psych. Review 102:684-704
- Note: Eddy reported ~95% of physicians answering 70-80%. The normative answer is 7.8%.

**`beauty_contest_mean`** — mean guess in a two-thirds beauty contest

- Value: 36 number 0-100 (medium)
- Source: Nagel (1995), American Economic Review 85:1313-1326
- Note: Nash equilibrium is 0. Human guesses spike at 33 (one step of reasoning) and 22 (two steps). Large newspaper samples average lower, around 23.

**`mini_ipip_agreeableness`** — mean Mini-IPIP agreeableness score

- Value: 4 1-5 scale (approximate)
- Source: Donnellan et al. (2006)

**`mini_ipip_conscientiousness`** — mean Mini-IPIP conscientiousness score

- Value: 3.4 1-5 scale (approximate)
- Source: Donnellan et al. (2006)

**`mini_ipip_extraversion`** — mean Mini-IPIP extraversion score

- Value: 3.2 1-5 scale (approximate)
- Source: Donnellan, Oswald, Baird & Lucas (2006), Psychological Assessment 18:192-203
- Note: Norms are sample-dependent; treat as a rough centre, not a target.

**`mini_ipip_neuroticism`** — mean Mini-IPIP neuroticism score

- Value: 2.8 1-5 scale (approximate)
- Source: Donnellan et al. (2006)

**`mini_ipip_openness`** — mean Mini-IPIP openness/intellect score

- Value: 3.7 1-5 scale (approximate)
- Source: Donnellan et al. (2006)

**`pd_cooperation_oneshot`** — cooperation rate in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma

- Value: 0.37 proportion (medium)
- Source: Sally (1995) meta-analysis, Rationality and Society 7:58-92; Mengel (2018) meta-analysis, Economic Journal 128:3182-3209
- Note: Estimates range roughly 0.30-0.50 depending on payoffs and framing.

**`pgg_round1_share`** — first-round contribution as share of endowment

- Value: 0.5 share of endowment (medium)
- Source: Ledyard (1995) in Handbook of Experimental Economics; Fehr & Gächter (2000), AER 90:980-994
- Note: Typically 40-60% in round 1, decaying toward zero over repeated rounds without punishment.

**`present_bias_reversal`** — preference reversal between immediate and delayed front end

- Value: 0.3 proportion (approximate)
- Source: Thaler (1981), Economics Letters 8:201-207; Frederick, Loewenstein & O'Donoghue (2002), JEL 40:351-401
- Note: Magnitude varies widely with amounts and delays; direction (more patience when both options are delayed) is the robust finding, not the level.

**`sunk_cost_continue`** — continuing the losing project

- Value: 0.85 proportion (medium)
- Source: Arkes & Blumer (1985), Org. Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35:124-140

**`ultimatum_rejection_low_offer`** — rejection rate for offers below 20% of pie

- Value: 0.5 proportion (medium)
- Source: Camerer (2003), Behavioral Game Theory, ch. 2
- Note: Rejection falls steeply as the offer rises; near-zero at an equal split.
